segments.title: The clock and the context
sections: The First Trade You Didn't Plan

cues.text: You sit down at 9:20. The open is already moving, the levels are stale, and a number printed at 8:30 that you never checked.
By 9:34 you are in a trade from the middle of the range, sized on a feeling, with a stop you placed after the fill.
That is a preparation problem, and the market has no say in preparation.
The fix is a sheet: one page, seven steps, the same order every session. A completed sheet clears you to trade.
Now, the clock. The routine ends at 9:25 a.m. Eastern, always.
The start moves. The finish does not. In your first weeks, expect about an hour, starting near 8:25. Once it is habit, about thirty minutes.
Slow? Start earlier. Never finish later. The open does not wait, and it has never once asked who was ready.
The rule: the sheet is finished by 9:25. A sheet still incomplete then means that session is watched, not traded.
Getting it wrong is still marking levels at 9:29. It reveals the start was set by when you woke up, not by how long the routine takes.
Now, step one. Context.
Context is where price sits before the open. Location, and only location, never a call on direction.
Three things. One: price against the prior-day range, the PD high and PD low. Above, inside or below.
Two: price against prior-day value, the PD VAH and PD VAL, the top and bottom of the prior day’s value area, where most of its volume traded.
Three: the overnight high and low, the ON high and ON low, and whether that range sits inside the prior day’s range or outside it.
Then short lines. The calendar, in nouns and dates: expiry Friday, roll week, a holiday. The room: how far an ordinary day travels, from the ATR.
The regime from Module 05: balance or imbalance, with its prices. And the gap, as a condition: gap if the open is above the PD high or below the PD low.
Never write bullish overnight, looks heavy, or a day-type label. A direction before the open is an opinion with nothing under it, and you will read every bar to agree with it.
The rule: context is written as location against named levels. It never carries a direction.
Getting it wrong is a line reading strong overnight, expecting higher. You are forecasting, and the forecast will decide your trades before price reaches a level.

cues.text: Step two: news. Before you open a chart, build the release list, with the times.
Tier One, the releases you go flat for. The inflation prints: CPI, PPI and PCE.
The jobs report, the Fed’s rate decision, and retail sales.
Each gets its time, its T minus five and its T plus two.
T minus five: five minutes before, flat, nothing resting at a level. T plus two: two minutes after, entries allowed again.
Tier Two, the smaller releases, goes on one line headed manage through. You do not exit a working position for them.
Take the times from the agency that publishes the number, not from memory.
One CPI line, in order. The alarm rings at 8:24. At 8:25, T minus five, you are flat.
At 8:30, CPI prints. At 8:31 a spike prints the overnight high, so that price goes on the line. The number itself never does.
At 8:32, T plus two: entries allowed again.
The rule: every Tier One release is on the sheet with T minus five and T plus two.
Getting it wrong is writing nothing down, then meeting a number at 10 a.m. with an order resting at a level.
It reveals a calendar read, not turned into times you act at. The fix: an alarm at T minus six.
Step three: levels. They come from one list, Module 06’s. Each has a slug, the short name you log it under, like pd-high.
VWAP, pivots, moving averages, Fibonacci levels and round numbers are not on the list. They are easy to draw. Price has not noticed.
Every level is a zone, a price band with two edges. The far edge is the one on the far side from where price arrives.
Above price, the far edge is the top. Below, the bottom. The stop goes behind it.
Overlapping levels become one zone naming every slug in it: one level, with more behind it.
Each row has three groups. One: slug, near edge, far edge.
Two: side of price, scope, the session it was built from, and column, location or target.
Three: the stop sentence. The stop goes behind this price because of what happened there.
The rule: only Module 06 levels, each a zone with its far edge.
Getting it wrong is a single price for a level. The stop then sits on the line, inside the noise. A row with a blank field is deleted.

cues.text: Step four: the idea. It is the whole point of the sheet.
An idea is a conditional statement, written before the session. It says what you will do if price reaches a place. It never says where price will go.
Three parts. One: the thesis. If price does X at level A, and trigger T fires, then level B is the target.
X is a behaviour you can see at the level, like acceptance, price holding beyond the zone, from Module 10.
T is a named trigger from Module 13, the bar event that puts you in. A thesis with no trigger is not written.
Two: the invalidation. A named price, judged on a candle close, where the thesis is wrong. It sits at or behind a zone’s far edge.
Three: the conviction, strong, moderate or thin, counted from three checks: the zone check, the path check, and the room-and-clock check.
Three points is strong.
Two is moderate.
One or none is thin, with a reason clause naming the check that failed.
Conviction does not change your size. Size comes from the grade, in one table, in Module 14.
Now, the second idea and the nothing case. You can write a second idea, usually the mirror at the other side of value.
Then the nothing case, the zone where neither idea applies. Between the PD VAL and PD VAH, with neither extreme tested: no trade.
It is often the most useful line on the sheet, and the only one that never needs a stop.

The rule: the idea is if-then at named levels, with a named trigger, a written invalidation and a counted conviction. No written invalidation means No Setup, the journal tag for a trade taken on feel.
Getting it wrong is looking for longs, with no price where it stops being true. It reveals a wish about direction, and with no invalidation you will hold it after the market has said no.
The fix: an idea line is accepted only with five things. If, a slug, a trigger, then, and an invalidation price. Miss one and the line is crossed out.

cues.text: Step five: the systems check. Six boxes. Each is ticked only after you have looked at the screen, never from memory.
One: data live. The platform shows connected, and the last trade time on your chart matches the clock.
Two: the 2R limit set. Your daily loss limit is at the account, at 2R, twice the risk on one trade, with the lock on. With no lock, the sheet says 2R is written, not enforced.
Three: chart templates. The session template ends at 4 p.m. Eastern, both the regular-hours one and the full-session one.
Four: contract month. The symbol in the order ticket is the contract you mean to trade. In roll week, read the month character by character.
Five: the order template matches the plan. A bracket, the stop and target that go in with the entry, with the stop resting. Automatic breakeven off. No trail.
Six: alerts. Two on every zone, one at the near edge and one at the far edge, sound on.
The rule: all six boxes ticked from the screen before 9:25.
Getting it wrong is finding out at 9:41 that the order went to the expiring month, or that the template moved your stop.
It reveals you trusted the prior session’s settings to still be this one’s. The platform did exactly what you told it. That is the problem.
Step six: the rehearsal. Run the written plan once, aloud, before the open.
Read the idea as a sequence of things that happen. Price reaches the zone.
You wait for the trigger.
You enter, with the stop behind the far edge.
Then the part people skip. The stop fills: minus 1R. You run the post-loss reset from Module 02, word for word, ending with its three questions aloud.
A second loss is minus 2R. The limit fires. You write the time and close the platform.
Rehearse the nothing case too. Price sits in the middle, and you do nothing. It is the hardest branch to carry out live, so it is the one most worth rehearsing.
The rule: run the plan once, aloud, with the loss path and the nothing case, before 9:25.
Getting it wrong is ticking the box because you know the plan. It reveals you rehearsed the entry and not the exit. The fix: three blanks, filled in after you say them. Three blanks, no tick.

cues.text: Step seven: readiness. It is the only step about you rather than the market, which is why it comes last.
Score your state on one line, 0 to 2, at the top of the sheet. Do you want to see what happens at your levels, or do you need it to go a certain way?
Two: curious about what the market will do at your levels.
One: neutral.
Zero: needing something from the market, for a reason that lives outside the chart.
It is data for the journal, not a gate. The completed sheet is what clears you.
The rule: a readiness score of 0, 1 or 2, with one line of reason, every session.
Getting it wrong has two forms. Writing 2 every time, so the journal has nothing to compare. Or leaving it blank on a bad morning, hiding the days you most need on the record.
Now, the worked sheet: a composite MNQ sheet, invented prices. It stops at 9:25, before the open.
Readiness 1, neutral. Started at 8:20. CPI at 8:30 makes it a Tier One day.
Context: price at 21,418, inside the prior-day range, 21,310 to 21,460, and inside value, 21,355 to 21,430.
The regime: balance, 21,355 to 21,430.
The news line: alarm at 8:24, T minus five at 8:25, CPI at 8:30, T plus two at 8:32.
The overnight high, 21,447, printed at 8:31, so that price sits on the line.
Eleven zones, each with its far edge, scope, column and stop sentence.

Idea one: if price accepts above the PD high zone and a Pause N Go, the Module 13 trigger, resumes upward, then the prior-week high. Invalidation: a five-minute close back below 21,454. Conviction: moderate.
Idea two mirrors it below the PD VAL zone. A level sits in its path, so conviction is thin.
The nothing case: between 21,358 and 21,454 without acceptance outside it. No trade.
The sheet did not need a view on whether CPI was good or bad, a guess at the range, or a direction. The busiest line on it is the one that says no trade.
The rule the sheet shows: everything on it is a location, a time, a condition or a setting. Finished at 9:21, it clears you.
Getting it wrong is a sheet that reads like a forecast. It reveals you wrote an opinion instead of a plan.

cues.text: Take your last five sessions. For each one, score one point for every line that was on paper before 9:25.
One: the finish time is written, and it is 9:25 or earlier.
Two: context as location only, plus the calendar, room, regime and open lines.
Three: news, every Tier One release with T minus five and T plus two.
Four: levels, every row a slug from Module 06’s list, with both edges, scope, column and stop sentence.
Five: the idea, if-then at a slug, with a trigger, an invalidation price and a counted conviction.
Six: systems, all six boxes ticked, alerts included.
Seven: rehearsal and readiness, three rehearsal lines filled and a score written.
Seven of seven is a complete sheet.
Anything less is incomplete, and a session traded off an incomplete sheet is the first thing to fix. Six of seven is not almost. It is a sheet with a hole in it.
The threshold: if two or more of your five sheets scored under seven, or any of them missed line five, the routine is not running yet.
Find the line you miss most often and fix that one first. The idea line comes before all others.
Getting it wrong is rounding six up to seven. It reveals the routine is a mood, not a sheet.
The assignment. Before your next session, copy the sheet onto one page and fill in one line: the news line.
Every Tier One release, its time, its T minus five and its T plus two, from the agency’s own schedule. That is the whole assignment.
In one line: seven steps, one sheet, finished by 9:25. A completed sheet clears you to trade. It never needs to know where price will go.
Where it goes next. The idea on the sheet is the plan from Module 15, Writing The Plan. The sheet is where it gets written each morning.
Module 17, The Session And The Close, picks up at 9:30: alerts at the levels on this sheet, the plan as the only input, and the end-of-day routine.
The readiness score and the finish time stay on the sheet as data.
In the weekly review in Module 18, you set the week’s sheets beside your grades and see whether your zero days look different from your two days.
The sources list the agency schedules the times come from. Where they disagree, the agency’s page wins.

check.q: How many of the seven lines make a complete sheet?
options: Four, if the idea is there
check.why: Seven of seven. Anything less is incomplete.

check.q: Which result means the routine is not running yet?
options: Two or more of five sheets under 7, or any miss on line five
check.why: Two or more under seven, or any miss on the idea line.

check.q: Which line do you fix first when you miss several?
check.why: The idea line comes before all others.

check.q: Counting six of seven as a pass reveals what?
options: The routine is a mood, not a sheet
check.why: Six of seven is incomplete.

questions.q: When does the pre-market routine end?
questions.why: The finish is fixed at 9:25. The start moves.

questions.q: Which word may a context line carry?
questions.why: Location words and level prices only.

questions.q: For a Tier One release, what is written beside the time?
questions.why: T−5 (flat) and T+2 (entries allowed again), plus any level it printed.

questions.q: For a level below price, where is the first-touch far edge?
questions.why: Below price, the far edge is the bottom. The stop goes behind it.

Where does each systems-check tick come from?
options: The screen in front of you
questions.why: Only a setting you have looked at.

questions.q: What is the readiness score used for?
questions.why: It is data, not a gate.

questions.q: A sheet scores 6 of 7. It is…
questions.why: Seven of seven is a complete sheet.
